sorular.soru: By definition, what exactly does an LLM do when it "generates the next token"?
secenekler: It finds the training sentence most similar to the context and copies its continuation word for word
It assigns a probability to every token in the vocabulary and samples one from that distribution
It extracts the grammar tree of the context and picks the word that best fits the grammatical rules
It looks up the correct answer in an internal knowledge base and writes the most reliable one found
sorular.aciklama: The model produces a P(next token | context) distribution, and generation means repeatedly sampling tokens from it. Finding and copying a training sentence is retrieval behavior; an LLM does not fetch memorized text, it assigns probabilities.

sorular.soru: What is the best interpretation of the "Probability ≠ truth" warning about language models?
secenekler: The model never produces low-probability tokens, so rare but correct facts are lost
Because softmax normalizes probabilities to sum to 1, no token can be considered fully correct
Probability assignment applies only in sampling mode; under greedy decoding the model gives a definite answer
High probability says a continuation is common in the training data; it does not guarantee that it is correct
sorular.aciklama: The model learns the continuations that are most frequent in its training text; being frequent does not make something true, and this is the root of hallucination. The normalization option misreads a mathematical property: probabilities summing to 1 says nothing about correctness.

sorular.soru: To give a trigram model a longer memory, a team switches to a 6-gram model trained on the same corpus. Why does this tend to make its estimates less reliable instead of better?
secenekler: Longer contexts match fewer training sequences exactly, so more of the counts are tiny or zero
Longer contexts force words to be split into subword pieces, so the word counts stop lining up
Longer contexts turn the chain rule into an approximation, so probabilities stop summing to one
Longer contexts get squeezed into one fixed-size vector, so the early words fade from memory
sorular.aciklama: A count-based model needs exact matches, and the longer the conditioning context, the rarer each exact sequence becomes, so widening the window trades the limited-context problem for worse sparsity. The fixed-size vector option describes the bottleneck of recurrent encoders, not anything a count table does.

sorular.soru: The probability of a whole sequence can be written as a product of next-token probabilities, each conditioned on the entire preceding prefix. Which statement about this decomposition is true?
secenekler: It is an approximation; because long-range dependencies are ignored, it shares the flaw of n-gram models
It holds only for decoder-only models; sequence probability is not defined for encoder-only architectures
It is an exact equality; so predicting the next token is equivalent to modeling the sequence distribution
It holds only when tokens are independent of each other; this condition fails in natural language text
sorular.aciklama: This is the chain rule of probability and holds exactly for any joint distribution; the approximation is the n-gram's truncation of the condition to the last few words. The independence assumption is the opposite: the product of conditionals already accounts for dependencies.

sorular.soru: In the example "The keys to the old cabinet ___ on the table", which weakness of n-gram models is shown, and how do neural models overcome it?
secenekler: Sparsity; neural models rescue unseen sequences from zero probability through smoothing
Long-range dependency; neural models can use a longer context instead of a fixed window
Polysemy; neural models keep different vectors for keys depending on its meaning
Out-of-vocabulary words; neural models recognize cabinet by splitting it into subparts
sorular.aciklama: A local window sees "cabinet ___" and predicts the singular "is"; the correct verb "are" requires the subject "keys", which lies far back, and that is a long-range dependency. Sparsity is a different weakness of n-grams (e.g. "quantum banana treaty"), and it is not what this example illustrates.

sorular.soru: A trigram model has seen the sequence "the cat sat" many times in its training data but has never seen "the kitten sat". what is the consequence for a pure n-gram model?
secenekler: The model uses the semantic similarity between kitten and cat to produce a low but nonzero probability
The model treats kitten as out-of-vocabulary and falls back to predicting from characters
The model automatically widens its context window and uses other sentences containing kitten
The model finds no reliable count for this sequence; to it, cat and kitten are two unrelated symbols
sorular.aciklama: A count-based model only knows exact matches; an unseen sequence has a count of zero, and there is no notion of similarity between words. The similarity option describes exactly the generalization that neural models gain from learned representations; n-grams cannot do this.

sorular.soru: What is the reason behind the statement that "tokenizer choice affects sequence length and cost"?
secenekler: Different tokenizers split the same text into different numbers of tokens, and the model computes per token
The tokenizer determines the number of model parameters; a larger vocabulary always means a larger model overall
The tokenizer determines the embedding dimension (d_model); longer tokens require larger vectors to store them
The tokenizer fixes the context window in terms of word count; short words take up more room in the window
sorular.aciklama: The model processes tokens, not raw text; the same sentence can be 7 or 12 tokens, which directly changes computation, context window usage, and price. Vocabulary size only affects the number of rows in the embedding table; it does not determine d_model or the context window.

sorular.soru: Which statement is true about the tokenizer splitting "unbelievability" as "un | believ | ability"?
secenekler: The tokenizer performs morpheme analysis; believ was chosen as a piece because it is a common English root
Subword splitting applies only to out-of-vocabulary words; words already in the vocabulary are never split
The split is an engineering choice to encode rare words with a limited vocabulary, not to analyze language
The tokenizer looks at meaning vectors to pick the most meaningful pieces; that is why ability stayed whole
sorular.aciklama: Tokenization is not linguistic analysis; it is an engineering choice. Pieces are determined by the vocabulary, which is why non-grammatical pieces like "believ" appear. The tokenizer never sees meaning vectors; embedding comes after tokenization.

sorular.soru: What is the key difference between an LLM's input embedding and its hidden state?
secenekler: The input embedding is learned beforehand with Word2Vec; the hidden state is read from the Transformer's own table
The input embedding has a different dimension for each token; the hidden state is reduced to a fixed d_model
The input embedding is used only in training; at inference the model starts directly from the hidden state
The input embedding is a context-independent table lookup; the hidden state is context-dependent after the layers
sorular.aciklama: The embedding table is a V × d_model lookup and always returns the same row for "bank"; a contextual representation only forms after passing through the Transformer layers. An LLM's embeddings are learned through the model's own training, not with Word2Vec; an embedding is not the same thing as Word2Vec.

sorular.soru: Why is it a limitation that Word2Vec produces a single vector for the word "bank", and by what mechanism do LLMs overcome it?
secenekler: A single vector cannot separate meanings; the LLM solves this by keeping a separate vocabulary entry for each meaning
A single vector cannot separate meanings; the LLM looks at surrounding tokens to produce a contextual representation
A single vector uses too much memory; the LLM solves this by shrinking the vocabulary with shared subword embeddings
A single vector cannot be updated during training; the LLM solves this with an embedding table updated by gradients
sorular.aciklama: Word2Vec gives one vector per word type, so "river bank" and "bank deposit" get the same representation; in an LLM the same input vector is transformed into A and B according to context in the Transformer layers. Keeping a separate vocabulary entry for each meaning would blow up the vocabulary and require enumerating meanings in advance; LLMs do not do this.

sorular.soru: What is the "bottleneck" problem of RNN-based seq2seq models, and how does attention address it?
secenekler: All input is squeezed into one fixed-size vector; attention lets each token access the relevant tokens directly
Computation is sequential, step by step; attention overcomes this bottleneck by distributing layers across multiple GPUs
The embedding table bloats as the vocabulary grows; attention shrinks the vocabulary with subword pieces and sharing
Gradients explode or vanish over long sequences; attention keeps the gradient stable with residual connections
sorular.aciklama: The encoder RNN must compress an entire 50-word sentence into a single hidden state, and older information fades; attention removes this compression and lets each token look wherever it needs. Sequential computation is a second problem of RNNs, but it is not the one called the bottleneck; distributing across GPUs is not attention's mechanism either.

sorular.soru: Which need does the "dog chased cat ≠ cat chased dog" example emphasize, and why did this need not arise separately in RNNs?
secenekler: Causal masking; RNNs cannot see the future anyway, so they needed no separate mask
Bidirectional reading; RNNs processed the sequence in both directions, so they already captured order
Positional information; RNNs process tokens in order anyway, so order information was naturally present
A larger vocabulary; RNNs work at the word level, so order information was encoded in the vocabulary
sorular.aciklama: Attention operates on a set and does not inherently know token order, which is why positional information is added to the Transformer separately. In an RNN, order came for free from step-by-step processing. Causal masking is a mechanism for hiding the future, not order information.

sorular.soru: A team has a labeled dataset for classifying customer reviews as positive/negative and does not need to generate long text. Which architecture family is most suitable, and why?
secenekler: Encoder-only; it suits bidirectional context-understanding tasks and is fine-tuned with labeled data
Decoder-only; the autoregressive objective can directly generate class labels as text
Encoder–decoder; reading the input and producing a label as output is a typical seq2seq task
Encoder-only; but because it is trained only with masked-token prediction, it needs no extra labels
sorular.aciklama: BERT-style models are fine-tuned with labeled data for "understanding" tasks (classification, sentiment, NER). The last option picks the right architecture but with the wrong reasoning: masked-token prediction is a pretraining objective, and classification still requires labeled fine-tuning.

sorular.soru: What would be the most important consequence if causal masking were removed when training a decoder-only model?
secenekler: The model would see bidirectional context and learn better representations; only inference would be slightly slower
The context window would effectively be halved, because without the mask half of the positions would be unusable
Softmax outputs would no longer sum to 1, and greedy or sampling decoding would break at generation time
The model would see the target token in its input and learn to copy it; at inference there is no future token
sorular.aciklama: In training the whole sentence is available; without the mask, "capital" is visible while predicting "capital", and the model copies instead of learning. At inference the future tokens do not exist, so training and usage conditions diverge. Bidirectional context is a property of encoder-only models and is unsuitable for generation.

sorular.soru: A user sends the same prompt twice to the same model, with unchanged weights, and gets two different continuations. After switching to greedy decoding, the output is identical on every run. Which explanation fits?
secenekler: Sampling perturbs the logits with fresh noise on every run; greedy decoding removes that noise
Sampling draws a token at random from a fixed distribution; greedy always takes its top token
Sampling nudges the weights a little after each draw; greedy decoding keeps the weights frozen
Sampling reshapes the distribution on every run; greedy decoding restores the original shape
sorular.aciklama: For a given context the model's distribution is the same on both runs; the variation comes only from the random draw, while greedy is deterministic because it always picks the highest-probability token. Reshaping the distribution is what temperature does, and it too is fixed for a given setting; no decoding choice alters the weights.

sorular.soru: Suppose a model gives mat .98, floor .02 at T = 0.5, and mat .63, floor .23, roof .14 at T = 2.0. What is the mechanism by which a high temperature flattens the distribution?
secenekler: A high T adds noise to the model's weights, so different logits come out for the same context every time
A high T allows multiple tokens to be drawn in sampling; the probability mass is split among them equally
A high T divides the logits by T, shrinking the gaps; the post-softmax distribution flattens
A high T adds low-probability tokens to the candidate list; at T = 0.5, roof was never a candidate
sorular.aciklama: Logits are divided by T: with T=2, 3, 1, 0 become 1.5, 0.5, 0, and because the gaps shrink, softmax flattens; with T=0.5 they become 6, 2, 0 and the distribution sharpens. Decoding does not change the model weights; roof is a candidate at every T, only its probability changes.

sorular.soru: During training, a model is confidently wrong: it puts nearly all probability on an incorrect token and almost none on the token that actually comes next. Compared with a case where the correct token gets moderate probability, how does the cross-entropy loss treat it?
secenekler: The loss is identical, since it only records whether the top-ranked token was the correct one
The loss is smaller, since a confident prediction is rewarded whichever token it happens to favor
The loss is capped at a fixed maximum, so both cases push the weights with about equal strength
The loss is far larger, since it follows the correct token's probability, so the push is stronger
sorular.aciklama: The loss is the negative log of the probability assigned to the correct token, so the less probability that token receives, the larger the loss and the stronger the pressure to update. It is not a right/wrong tally of the top token: two wrong predictions can carry very different losses.

sorular.soru: The news story "How strangers got my email address from ChatGPT's model" is most directly related to which step of the pretraining data pipeline, and why?
secenekler: Dedup; repeated text gets memorized, and personal data in the training set can resurface in output
Lang ID; incorrect language detection lets personal data slip past the language filter and into the corpus
Mixture; if the share of web data in the mixture is high, the amount of personal information increases
Tokenize; email addresses are encoded as single tokens, so the model remembers them easily afterwards
sorular.aciklama: Filtering decisions affect memorization; repeated text gets memorized, and this is the technical source of the privacy risk. Mixture can indirectly affect the amount of personal information, but the step that explains memorization is deduplication.

sorular.soru: Two teams train with the same fixed budget of GPU time. One spends it on a very large model that sees comparatively little text; the other trains a smaller model on far more text and reaches a lower loss. Which idea best explains this outcome?
secenekler: Smaller models always generalize better, so adding parameters past some point raises the loss
Data size is the only factor that matters; parameters contribute little once training has begun
Under a fixed budget, size and data trade off; a big model shown too little text is undertrained
Compute is set by the tokenizer, so the two teams did not really spend the same training budget
sorular.aciklama: Compute pays for both parameters and training tokens, so pouring a fixed budget into parameters alone leaves the model starved of data; compute-optimal training scales the two together. The message is balance, not that smaller is always better: with more compute the larger model could be given enough data as well.

sorular.soru: When "Explain the moon landing to a 6-year-old" is given to a base model that has finished pretraining, the model lists similar questions instead of answering. What is the cause of this behavior?
secenekler: The model has not learned about the moon landing; continued pretraining with domain data is needed
The model is trained to continue text; instruction tuning teaches the question → answer format
The decoding temperature is too high; if lowered, the model would give a direct, coherent answer
The context window is full; unable to take in new information, the model repeats patterns it has seen
sorular.aciklama: A base LM answers the question "what would plausibly follow this text on the internet?", and what follows a question is often more questions; instruction and preference tuning teach the format and the behavior. It is a lack of format, not a lack of knowledge: the model most likely learned the facts during pretraining.
